title: Engagement

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was shidduch, and your line was a match: an introduction made with care, the yes left to the two. Today the match turns into a plan.

A plain china plate, wrapped in a cloth napkin. Two women, the mothers of the bride and the groom, each take an edge. A few minutes earlier, a short document was read aloud and signed in this room. Now, at a signal, they bring the plate down hard on the back of a chair. It shatters inside the napkin. People clap and call out mazel tov. At some Ashkenazi weddings, this happens shortly before the ceremony. The document is today's word, and the broken plate is its exclamation mark.
screen: `A PLATE IN A NAPKIN.` → `TWO MOTHERS, ONE SIGNAL.` → `IT SHATTERS. MAZEL TOV.`

segments.voice: Tena'im means conditions. It's an engagement agreement, setting down in writing what the two sides have agreed: that there will be a wedding, and what each family will bring to it. In earlier generations it could be signed long before the wedding. Today, couples who keep the custom often sign it on the wedding day itself, in a side room before the ceremony. Why agree at all? The prophet Amos asks a question that sounds written for an engagement: "Can two walk together, except they be agreed?" A marriage is two people on a long road, side by side. The tena'im says, before the walking starts: here is what we have agreed, out loud, in front of others. And the plate? Explanations differ, and families keep the custom without settling them. Some say it's a warning: a broken engagement, like a broken plate, can't be glued back, so treat this promise seriously. Others hear the same note as the glass broken under the canopy, a memory inside joy, which comes in a few days. Some couples now write tena'im in their own words, about how they hope to share a home, make decisions, disagree, and keep learning. The old idea holds. Conditions aren't a sign of distrust. They're how two people say plainly what they are building, before they build it.
screen: `AN AGREEMENT, IN WRITING.` · `CAN TWO WALK TOGETHER?` · `A PLATE THAT CAN'T BE GLUED.` · `TERMS IN THEIR OWN WORDS.` · then, large: `CONDITIONS.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone you share part of your life with, and one thing the two of you are building, even something small, like a weekly dinner. Notice what each of you has assumed about it but never said, and shape one condition you'd like to agree on out loud until it fits in one kind sentence.
Tena'im: conditions. The engagement agreement, read and signed, and at some weddings sealed with a broken plate. Today's word.
Your line: conditions. Agreeing out loud is a way of caring, not of doubting. Until tomorrow.
